children: Solid growth and earnings weren't enough for Zebra Technologies investors this quarter. Memory chip prices are hitting profitability, even as the company works to pass through higher costs.

On Tuesday, the maker of productivity and automation software and hardware reported third-quarter earnings per share of $4.95, up 28% year over year, from sales of $1.6 billion, up 22% year over year. Wall Street was looking for earnings per share of $4.89 from sales of $1.6 billion.
Numbers look solid. So does guidance.
For the fourth quarter, Zebra expects sales growth of between 10% and 14%. Wall Street currently projects fourth-quarter sales of $1.6 billion, up 9% year over year.
Still, shares were down 9.2% in early trading at $327.91, while the S&P 500 was up 0.3% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 0.7%.

The drop came despite management indicating that 2027 sales would be near the higher end of the company's 5% to 7% long-term annual sales growth target. That's a little better than current Wall Street estimates.
The problem boils down to margins. Zebra sees 2027 operating margins at roughly 20% to 21%. Wall Street is modeling closer to 22%.
The weaker margins are partly due to higher memory chip costs that are being passed through to customers. Zebra's absolute operating profit earned in 2027 should be close to Wall Street estimates.
Still, higher prices are a headwind for demand, although CEO Bill Burns tells Barron's that customer activity has been unaffected by recent price increases.

Expectations for Zebra's earnings were also running high. Coming into Tuesday trading, Zebra stock was up 49% this year. Shares jumped 27% after the company beat second-quarter earnings per share estimates by 46%. This earnings beat topped the Street by just 1%, but estimates rose roughly 35 cents after the strong second-quarter results.
Whatever the reason, investors don't appear happy with a more modest beat-and-raise quarter from the company.
